User: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Coastal Manufacturing: $68,200. Additional income: $16,300 (photography, 3 clients), $2,100 from Capital One 360, $420 from Merrill Edge. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 740 sq ft. Deductions: $5,100 student loan interest (Nelnet, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have receipt; $1,050 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to tr

eat the home office, and what forms I need?
Assistant: I can walk you through what’s deductible, whether you should itemize, how to treat the home office, and which forms you’ll likely need. I’m not a CPA — consider this general guidance and consult a tax professional for definitive filing decisions. A few quick clarifying questions are at the end so I can give a tighter answer or run sample calculations.

Summary answers up front
- Likely take the 2024 standard deduction (single) unless you have other item

izable items you haven’t listed — with the items you gave, standard deduction will probably be larger.
- Your photography income is self-employment income and should be reported on Schedule C; you’ll also owe self-employment tax (Schedule SE).
- Home office: you can claim a deduction for the business use of your rented home. The “actual expense” method (allocating a portion of rent) almost certainly gives a bigger deduction than the simplified method for your numbers, but you can choose either. Use Form 882

9 if you pick actual expenses.
- You’ll need Form 1040 plus Schedule C, Schedule SE, and likely Schedule B (because your interest totals exceed $1,500). Also collect any 1099s or 1098-E (student loan interest) you receive.

Details and calculations

1) Which income goes where
- W-2 from Coastal Manufacturing ($68,200): reported on Form 1040 using the W-2.
- Photography ($16,300): report on Schedule C (business income). If you get 1099-NEC or 1099-K from clients, include those amounts but you must report all

income even if you don’t get a 1099.
- Bank/broker interest ($2,100 + $420 = $2,520): taxable interest; reported on Form 1040. Because your total taxable interest (or ordinary dividends) exceeds $1,500, you’ll generally need Schedule B.

2) Home office (120 sq ft, exclusive; home = 740 sq ft; rent $1,750/month)
- Qualification: To deduct, the space must be used regularly and exclusively for business and be your principal place of business (or used to meet clients, etc.). From what you wrote, it sounds like

it qualifies.
- Two methods:
  - Simplified method: $5 per sq ft × 120 sq ft = $600 deduction (no Form 8829).
  - Actual expense method: allocate a portion of actual home expenses by the business-use percentage. Percentage = 120 / 740 ≈ 16.22%. Annual rent = $1,750 × 12 = $21,000. Rent portion = 21,000 × 16.22% ≈ $3,405. (If you have utilities, renter’s insurance, etc., their business shares would add to this when using actual-expense method.)
- Recommendation (based on numbers you gave): The actual-expens

e method (≈ $3,405 rent portion) is substantially better than the simplified $600; you should use actual-expense method unless you expect depreciation or other complications to change the math. If you choose actual expenses, use Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) and report the allocated amounts on Schedule C.

3) Self-employment tax and related deductions
- Net profit from Schedule C (gross photography income minus allowable business expenses including the home-office allocation) is subject

to self-employment (SE) tax.
- SE tax is computed on net earnings (roughly 92.35% of net profit) at about 15.3% (Social Security + Medicare). You then get an “above-the-line” deduction on Schedule 1 for one-half of the self-employment tax.
- Example (rounded) to show impact of home-office choice:
  - With simplified home-office ($600): Schedule C net ≈ $16,300 − $600 = $15,700. SE tax ≈ $2,220; half SE deduction ≈ $1,110.
  - With actual home-office ($3,405): Schedule C net ≈ $16,300 − $3,405 = $12,895. SE

tax ≈ $1,823; half SE deduction ≈ $911.
  - So actual method reduces both your net taxable business income and your SE tax — it’s beneficial here.

4) Student loan interest ($5,100) — important clarification needed
- The student loan interest deduction (up to $2,500 per year) is an adjustment to income (reported on Schedule 1) and is allowed only for interest paid in the tax year you’re filing for. It’s subject to an income-based phaseout.
- Clarify: Are the $5,100 payments interest paid in 2024, or are th

ose payments from earlier years (2018–2021)? If they were paid in prior years, they’re not deductible on your 2024 return. If you paid $5,100 in 2024, the maximum deductible for 2024 would still be $2,500 (subject to AGI limitations) and you’ll need Form 1098-E from your servicer (Nelnet).

5) Charitable contributions ($1,500)
- Deductible if you itemize (keep your receipt). Cash donation to a qualifying charity is an itemized deduction.
- But because the standard deduction for a single taxpayer in 2024 is

likely around $14,600, your $1,500 contribution alone won’t make itemizing worthwhile unless you have other deductible items (mortgage interest, large property taxes, large medical expenses above the threshold, etc.).

6) Unreimbursed expenses ($1,050)
- If these are unreimbursed employee expenses from a W-2 job — not deductible for federal returns under current law (TCJA suspended miscellaneous itemized deductions through 2025).
- If they are business expenses related to your photography self-employment, t

hey should be claimed on Schedule C (and reduce your Schedule C net income).

7) Other forms you may need
- 1040 (U.S. Individual Income Tax Return)
- Schedule 1 (Additional Income and Adjustments) — for adjustments such as half of SE tax and student loan interest
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — for photography income and business expenses
- Schedule SE (Self-Employment Tax)
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) — only if you use actual expenses for the home office
- Schedule B

— if taxable interest or ordinary dividends > $1,500
- Form(s) 1099-NEC / 1099-K (if clients issued them), 1099-INT (bank interest), 1099-DIV or 1099-B from Merrill Edge if applicable
- Form 8949 / Schedule D if you sold securities with capital gains/losses (check your Merrill Edge statements)

8) Estimated tax payments
- Because you have self-employment income, you may need to make quarterly estimated tax payments to cover income tax and self-employment tax (avoid penalties). If you had little or no withho

ldings to cover the additional tax from your self-employment income and interest, you could owe tax at filing time.

What I recommend you do next (checklist)
- Confirm whether the $5,100 student loan interest was paid in 2024 (and get Form 1098-E from Nelnet if so).
- Categorize the $1,050 unreimbursed expenses: business-related (Schedule C) or employee-related (probably not deductible).
- Gather documents: W-2, 1099-NEC/K, 1099-INT, Merrill’s consolidated 1099 (dividends/interest/1099-B), receipts for char

itable gifts, receipts for business expenses, rent statements (annual rent), and a floorplan or measurement showing the 120 sq ft office area.
- Decide home-office method: based on your numbers, actual-expense method (with Form 8829) will likely give a larger deduction.
- If you’d like, I can run a more precise tax-estimate (rough AGI, estimated federal tax, and SE tax) using either home-office method — tell me whether the student loan interest payments were in 2024 and whether the $1,050 expenses are busin

ess-related.

Would you like me to:
- (A) do a full sample calculation/estimate of 2024 federal tax (using the actual-home-office and simplified methods side-by-side), or
- (B) just prepare a checklist and sample Form list you can give to a tax preparer?

If you want the sample calculation, please confirm:
1) Were any of the student loan interest payments made in 2024 (and if so, how much in 2024)?  
2) Are the $1,050 unreimbursed expenses business-related (photography) or employee-related (W-2 job)?  
3) A
ny other deductible items not mentioned (mortgage interest, property taxes, large medical expenses, IRA contributions, HSA)?
